expectations.text: The reply opens with the recommendation and does not put the whole product and engineering organisation on the rebrand: it protects capacity for the top customer problems.
expectations.evidence: 'Plan Q1 so the rebrand lands on a product that works, not instead of fixing it... My proposal: the new name in the app and the marketing site ship in Q1; the design system starts on the invoicing and reports screens...; the domain moves in Q2; the rest of capacity goes to the three complaints.'

expectations.text: The reply splits the rebrand into a small must-have part (for example the name in the app, domain redirects, legal text) and parts that can wait or be phased (for example a full design system), and makes the cost of each visible.
expectations.evidence: Name and site in Q1, the design system phased (starting on the invoicing and reports screens), the domain moved to Q2. Cost: 'Have the teams estimate the rebrand pieces and the fixes'; the options show 'what ships, what waits, revenue at risk'; the domain is flagged as 'costly to undo'; 'The marketing site is mostly marketing and web work, not product engineering.'

expectations.text: The reply ranks the customer problems with evidence (for example NPS comments, churn or revenue at risk, support tickets) and sets measures for fixing them.
expectations.evidence: 'Revenue from accounts that raised the three complaints, how much renews in Q1-Q2, and detractor comments by theme.' Measures: 'Give every item an outcome: invoice run time, integration sync success rate, report-related tickets, NPS of the complaining accounts. Review monthly with leadership.'

expectations.text: The reply brings leadership options with explicit trade-offs instead of a flat no.
expectations.evidence: 'Write one page with three options. A: whole organisation on the rebrand. B: the split above. C: fixes first, rebrand in Q2. For each: what ships, what waits, revenue at risk, what customers see. Recommend B.'

expectations.text: The reply handles "leadership decides, teams execute" and "any decision beats no decision" constructively: a private conversation first, asking for the reasons, separating decisions that are cheap to reverse from ones that aren't, and offering a light decision process, without labelling or attacking the leaders.
expectations.evidence: 'Then take it to the CEO privately (your own manager first, if that isn't the CEO), before any leadership meeting. Ask for the reasons, not a reversal: what's driving the Q1 date, and what would change their mind?' It singles out the domain as 'costly to undo' and moves it until after the integration is stable, offers a one-page options paper and a monthly review, and says 'Any decision beats no decision, agreed... I'll execute whichever you choose.' The reversibility split is applied to the domain rather than spelled out against the slogan.

expectations.text: The reply is practical and short enough to act on (roughly 500 words or less), with any longer plan offered or attached as a separate document.
expectations.evidence: 445 words (wc -w), action-ordered, with an offer to draft the options paper.

factual_errors.evidence: The domain-change effects (OAuth redirect URIs, webhooks, SSO, API URLs and allowlists, sending reputation of invoice emails) are accurate. 'NPS fell 24 points' is correct. No wrong claims found.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: No leader says the responsibility for the NPS fall or the open complaints is leadership's.

best_insight.value: It moves the domain change to Q2, after the integration is stable, and starts the design system on the invoicing and reports screens, so the first new-brand screens customers see are ones that now work.

suggestions.assertion: The reply handles "leadership decides, teams execute" and "any decision beats no decision" constructively: a private conversation first, asking for the reasons, separating decisions that are cheap to reverse from ones that aren't, and offering a light decision process, without labelling or attacking the leaders.
suggestions.reason: This assertion bundles four required behaviours plus a tone check. Several strong samples met three of the four and failed on one (usually asking for the reasons, or splitting reversible from irreversible decisions). Splitting it into two assertions would give a clearer signal.

No assertion checks the technical link between the new domain and the broken accounting integration (OAuth redirect URIs, webhooks, sending-domain reputation, customer allowlists). Most samples raised it, and it is the most practical sequencing argument. Capacity realism (no overtime, slack for incidents) and committing to the decision once it is made also go unchecked.

eval_feedback.overall: Meets every assertion in under 450 words, with the most concrete phasing of the rebrand.
